entities.summary:
Adam Reißner (also spelled Reusner or Reissner), born in Mindelheim around 1500, emerged as a prominent German mystic, hymn-writer, and poet during the tumultuous Early Modern period, profoundly shaping the spiritual and literary landscape of the Protestant Reformation. His life, spanning from 1500 to 1572, placed him at the heart of intellectual and religious ferment in Western Europe, where he navigated the seismic shifts of theological debate and the burgeoning print culture, becoming a significant voice in the development of vernacular sacred song. Reißner is particularly remembered for his contributions to German hymnody, which provided accessible spiritual comfort and theological instruction to the common people in an era of profound religious change.

Educated at the universities of Ingolstadt and Heidelberg, Reißner initially pursued a path in humanistic studies before embracing the burgeoning Protestant movement, albeit with a distinct mystical bent. His most enduring literary achievement is the collection of hymns, many of which were first published in the widely influential Strasbourg hymnals of the mid-16th century. Notably, his hymn "Ich armer Mensch, ich armer Sünder" ("I, poor man, I, poor sinner") became a staple of Protestant worship, embodying the era's focus on personal penitence and divine grace. Beyond hymns, Reißner penned theological treatises and mystical writings, often reflecting a deep, introspective piety that resonated with both Lutheran and Anabaptist circles, bridging different Protestant currents through shared spiritual experience.

His work helped democratize religious understanding and left a lasting imprint on German literature.
